detail.abstract: Food systems are complex, involving interdependencies, path dependence, and partly unforeseeable social-ecological feedback among stakeholders. These factors make transformative pathways uncertain and unpredictable. Value chains, as a problem domain, can either impede or empower stakeholders to implement sustainable practices. They represent a meso-level where institutional coordination has the potential to address these issues by scaling up and scaling deep. However, achieving a contextualized fit for agri-food meso-level coordination in transformation is challenging. Coordination initiatives emerge from mixed institutional logics and rely on existing institutional developments, leading to diverse pathways of sustainability amplification. This paper takes stock of research gaps identified in institutional, innovation, and social-ecological literature. It emphasizes the need to address the institutional fit for sustainability amplification through a contextualized assessment of stakeholder coordination. To this end, the paper theoretically anchors a model of value chain organizing (MVCO) in a contextualized combination of complex features of institutional coordination. We propose a configurational MVCO that articulates dimensions and outcomes of contextual fit in both static and dynamic interplay. We discuss the model's significance from explanatory, interpretative, and emancipatory perspectives. Additionally, we identify the model's adaptive potential for empirical inquiry into stakeholder coordination in agri-food and beyond, across interdisciplinary and transdisciplinary endeavors.

detail.abstract: Global manufacturing and services are evolving due to automation driven by artificial intelligence. There are two aspects to the opportunities facing emerging markets. On one hand, AI has the potential to foster development, enhance productivity, and generate new exports and services. On the other hand, insufficient digital infrastructure, variations in technological skills, and a shortage of qualified workers may lead to the concentration of benefits within a limited segment of the economy, exacerbating inequality. To explore the impacts of the transition in the labor market, this research establishes a foundational computational simulation framework, integrates existing research and theory, and outlines an empirical method for validating model forecasts using cross-national data. The primary findings from the evidence assessment and simulation suggest that the implementation of AI boosts overallthe pace of reallocation relies on the rate of skill enhancement, the composition of sectors within the economy, and national policy reactions. Policy initiatives that integrate focused investment in digital infrastructure, extensive reskilling efforts, social safety nets for affected workers, and incentives for local innovation can boost the proportion of benefits accrued by emerging economies.

title: Technological Diffusion and Global Convergence: The Circulation of Innovation from Advanced to Developing Economies

detail.title: Technological Diffusion and Global Convergence: The Circulation of Innovation from Advanced to Developing Economies

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the research, writing, or conclusions of this paper.

detail.abstract: Technological innovation is no longer the sole domain of a few advanced economies—it is diffusing globally at unprecedented speed. This paper examines how breakthroughs in automation, artificial intelligence (AI), financial technology (fintech), healthcare, energy, agriculture, and digital infrastructure are spreading from technology leaders to developing economies, and how this diffusion is driving economic convergence. We draw on diffusion theory and case studies (with an emphasis on African economies) to illustrate “leapfrogging” in action, where latecomer nations bypass traditional development stages by adopting cutting-edge solutions. We find that global technology circulation, enabled by falling costs and intensified knowledge flows, is reshaping productivity and living standards at scale. In many developing regions, access to mobile connectivity, renewable energy, digital finance, and AI-powered services has expanded dramatically, boosting growth and lifting millions from poverty. However, we also discuss challenges—such as digital divides and capacity gaps—that affect how quickly and equitably these benefits are realized. The 21st century, we argue, will be defined not only by the emergence of new technologies, but by how swiftly and inclusively they diffuse across the world.

title: Mandatory AI-Risk Disclosure as a Signalling Device in Capital Markets

detail.title: Mandatory AI-Risk Disclosure as a Signalling Device in Capital Markets

contentType.other: This is a paper submitted to UCL Explore Econ research Conference 2025. I intend to preprint this paper here.

detail.abstract: Recent regulatory initiatives such as the EU Artificial Intelligence Act and the SEC's proposed rules on predictive data analytics aim to counter "AI-washing" by mandating audited disclosure of firms' AI capabilities. This paper analyses how mandatory AI-risk disclosure regimes function as signalling mechanisms in capital markets. Using a simplified signalling-game framework with random audits, disclosure costs, and penalties, it examines when genuine AI firms truthfully disclose while hype-oriented firms hide or exaggerate. The model shows that separating equilibria, where only genuine AI leaders disclose, emerge when audit probabilities and penalties are sufficiently high relative to compliance costs; otherwise, firms may pool at non-disclosure, defeating the policy's intent. Comparative statics indicate that moderate enforcement can improve welfare by enhancing market trust without overburdening smaller innovators. The results highlight a regulatory trade-off: ensure credible transparency without deterring genuine innovation.

detail.abstract:
Minimal Support Price (MSP) has been a major aspect of the Indian agricultural policy to support farmers in terms of price stability and income supplement. The argument about the sustainability of agriculture and the long-term goals of the country development as suggested in Viksit Bharat 2047 has demonstrated that the legal guarantee of the MSP has taken a new dimension. The authors of this article state the economic implications of a legally binding MSP, in particular, its ability to reorganize the economic incentives to produce, and to enhance the welfare of farmers, and stabilize the livelihoods of the rural regions. One of the key considerations that have been examined is that of MSP in diversifying other crops other than rice-wheat practices to bring about more sustainable and climate resilient practices. A legal and economic approach informs the speculation on the way the implementation of a legally stipulated MSP system would advance the food security, resource management and fair able market practices. This paper is of the view that, though the legal support may be reliable in the short run, its execution would be dependent on the alignment of the MSP policies with the diversification 
policies,  the investments in the rural infrastructures and the open procurement practices. The study contributes to the policy discussion because it gives the contextualization of MSP as a piece of the broader agenda of agricultural transformation and inclusive development leading to Viksit Bharat 2047.

detail.abstract:
This article studies and explains the reasons for the role of cross-dressing in disturbing the Islamic system and its sub-systems. For the purpose, we referred to the theories and conceptual frameworks provided by some religious thinkers like Allameh Tabatabaei, Shahid Motahari, and Ayatollah Mesbah Yazdi, and sketched a normative Islamic model for personal, family, and social systems. For explaining the fundamental role of gender and sexual differences in the formation of this normative model, four major concepts of primordial human nature (fitrah), justice, duality, and sexual identity, are introduced by reference to Qur’anic sources. In the end, beside the rational analysis of sexual and gender implications of these systems, we show that cross-dressing introduces disorder into various levels of identity, on one hand, and disrupts the desired religious system and order, on the other. This article uses interpretive-rational method in the sketching of the characteristics of a normative Islamic model. The analysis of the hypotheses and rational explanations were done by rational method and examining it against social theories.

detail.title: GDP Nowcasting Performance of Traditional Econometric Models vs Machine-Learning Algorithms

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Are Machine Learning (ML) algorithms superior to traditional econometric models for GDP nowcasting in a time series setting? Based on our evaluation of all models from both classes ever used in nowcasting across simulation and six country cases, traditional econometric models tend to outperform ML algorithms. Among the ML algorithms, linear ML algorithm – Lasso and Elastic Net – perform best in nowcasting, even surpassing traditional econometric models in cases of long GDP data and rich high-frequency indicators. Among the traditional econometric models, the Bridge and Dynamic Factor deliver the strongest empirical results, while Three-Pass Regression Filter performs well in our simulation. Due to the relatively short length of GDP series, complex and non-linear ML algorithms are prone to overfitting, which compromises their out-of-sample performance.

title: Good News Travels Fast
affiliations: Central Bank of Chile, ,  and International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: Good News Travels Fast

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: In this paper we study how aggregate demand surprises affect and propagate to the global economy, with particular attention to their impact on Emerging Market Economies (EMEs). To do so, we introduce a new high-frequency external instrument to identify global demand shocks: the sensitivity of oil futures prices around labor market announcements from the US and the Euro Area, two events that consistently trigger strong revisions in global growth expectations across financial markets. Using a proxy-SVAR framework, our results suggest that a global demand shock has positive effects on world industrial production, reduces oil inventories and global uncertainty, and improves financial conditions. In EMEs, upward revision in macroeconomic outlook leads to higher industrial production and inflation, real exchange rate appreciation, and lower EMBI spreads. When the sample is split between oil-importers and exporters, we observe results consistent with the role of external trade exposure in shaping transmission, heterogeneity in the magnitude and persistence of output, inflation, real exchange rates, and sovereign risk responses. These results are consistent with theoretical expectations and the related literature. Our findings offer a credible empirical strategy for isolating global demand shocks and have direct implications for empirical macroeconomic modeling of emerging market economies.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the macro-criticality of water resources in the context of climate change. It summarizes the past and future trends of water scarcity and droughts and proposes a framework to analyze the macro-criticality and role of public sector engagement in the water sector. The paper maps out channels through which water resources affect the macro-fiscal and balance of payments positions and develops an understanding of macro-fiscal exposure based on empirical evidence. It also synthesizes emerging insights from IMF-supported operations and capacity development activities, thereby clarifying the rationale and scope for IMF engagement in water-related policy reforms.

title: The Food and Agriculture Sector in IMF Publications
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF) and

detail.title: The Food and Agriculture Sector in IMF Publications

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper presents a text-mining analysis of discussions of food and agriculture issues in publications of the International Monetary Fund's (IMF) from 1946 to mid-2025, with deeper analysis on subsets of this period for selected publication types. It examines how references to food security and agriculture (FSA) have evolved over time, assesses how they differ across IMF outlets and regional focus of the papers, and explores the coverage of subtopics of FSA as well as broader economic contexts within which FSA is contextualized. Using text data from the IMF’s eLibrary metadata as well as its full-text data processed through the use of the Fund Document Extraction Toolkit (FDET), the study identifies key trends in the frequency and intensity of FSA references. The results indicate that IMF attention to FSA issues tends to peak during periods of global food crises and significant agricultural policy changes. These peaks closely track inflationary trends with minimal lag, suggesting rapid response of IMF work to crises. The study also reveals regional variations, with Sub-Saharan Africa and Emerging and Developing Asia exhibiting the highest prevalence of FSA references, while advanced economies show lower prevalence. The analysis also finds that FSA-focused publications exhibit greater attention to selected core macroeconomic themes (inflation and trade) as well as to newer thematic areas (climate change and inequality) relative to other IMF work. The tools and methods can be applied to macrocritical dimensions of other sectoral concerns, and the findings provide a foundation for further research that can extend the methodology and content of this work.

title: Carbon Risk in Loan Pricing

detail.title: Carbon Risk in Loan Pricing

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We study how carbon risk affects the pricing of U.S. corporate loans and how firms’ and lenders’ commitments influence both loan terms and business decisions. Combining syndicated loan data with firm-level carbon emissions, we document a carbon risk premium: financial institutions charge higher loan risk spreads to borrowers with a higher carbon intensity. This premium varies with the environmental commitments of borrowers and lenders. Borrowers signaling commitments—emission targets, emission disclosures, or green loans—receive discounts that decline with increasing carbon intensity, while committed lenders charge higher interest rates to carbon-intensive borrowers. Beyond affecting the carbon premium, commitments influence real economic outcomes by increasing corporate investment and R&D expenditures, and by reducing precautionary liquidity holdings. We also show that the carbon premium in U.S. loan markets intensifies during periods of monetary tightening in line with the risk-taking channel of monetary policy. Notably, the carbon premium is time varying and has declined in recent years.

detail.abstract: The classification of shareholder proposals into environmental, social, and governance (ESG) categories by human analysts is subject to ambiguity and inconsistency, which undermines the reliability of empirical research and policy applications. This study introduces a novel approach that leverages large language models’ domain knowledge to systematically categorize shareholder proposals into ESG dimensions. The method minimizes subjectivity in classification and strengthens comparability across studies. Moreover, the framework is fully replicable and adaptable, allowing researchers and practitioners to extend the approach to other ESG-related taxonomies and governance contexts.

detail.abstract: This study aims to analyze the implementation of the Statement of Financial Accounting Standards (PSAK) 210 concerning events after the reporting period and its role in supporting transparency and sustainability in financial reporting among public companies in Indonesia. The research employs a descriptive qualitative approach using a literature study based on previous research findings and official publications from the Indonesian Institute of Accountants (IAI). The results indicate that although PSAK 210 is conceptually aligned with the International Accounting Standard (IAS) 10 issued by the International Accounting Standards Board (IASB), its implementation in Indonesia remains inconsistent. Many public companies disclose post-reporting events only in general terms without providing adequate quantitative details, leading to information asymmetry between companies and investors. The findings imply that effective application of PSAK 210 is essential to strengthen transparency, accountability, and corporate governance. Therefore, improved regulatory oversight, auditor competence, and managerial awareness are required to ensure that post-reporting event disclosures reflect the integrity and sustainability of financial reporting in Indonesia.

detail.abstract: Zara's successful strategies set a valuable example for other brands aiming to achieve and maintain a competitive edge. Zara, a renowned fashion retailer under Inditex, is widely recognized for its products for both men and women. Zara has successfully utilized a combination of traditional marketing methods and behavioral economics principles to boost brand loyalty, increase sales, and improve the overall customer experience. By incorporating tactics like pricing strategies, time-limited promotions, social proof, and choice architecture, Zara has established an appealing shopping environment that connects with consumers both logically and emotionally. Despite strong competitors like H&M, Zara consistently holds the top spot worldwide. Recent data shows Zara's impressive net profit and projected growth, attributed to its strong market presence, sales, and global expansion. With an efficient supply chain and effective positioning, Zara has become a preferred brand. Although Zara is wellestablished, its presence in India is mainly limited to its metropolitan areas, with many consumers unfamiliar with the brand. title: Foundation-Model Governance Pathways: From Preference Models to Operative Rules
affiliations: Universidad de la Republica

detail.title: Foundation-Model Governance Pathways: From Preference Models to Operative Rules
detail.abstract:
Current research on foundation model alignment concentrates on preference optimization and reward model design, yet it does not explain how these mechanisms become enforceable linguistic structures in model outputs. This paper introduces a formal bridge between training choices and governance-level effects by defining the operative rule as a compiled constraint that determines which clause types a model may produce. The framework maps policy inputs such as statutes, institutional directives, and redline restrictions into a preference graph over clause types, then compiles those directives into executable constraints that control decoding. It proposes measurable clause-level metrics including coverage, leakage, authority-bearing density, and constraint satisfaction, together with an auditable chain of custody that links governance inputs to observable textual outcomes. Cross-domain simulations in healthcare, securities disclosure, and administrative reporting demonstrate how governance parameters can be enforced without access to proprietary weights. The result is a verifiable clause calculus that operationalizes accountability and replaces abstract alignment narratives with testable governance artifacts connecting preference models to the operative law embedded in generated text.

title: Contextual Determinants of Hurricane Preparedness in a Small Island Developing State: Insights from Hurricane Beryl in St. Vincent and the Grenadines

detail.title: Contextual Determinants of Hurricane Preparedness in a Small Island Developing State: Insights from Hurricane Beryl in St. Vincent and the Grenadines
detail.abstract: As climate change accelerates, Small Island Developing States (SIDS) are increasingly vulnerable to more frequent and severe hurricanes. This paper examines hurricane preparedness, response, and recovery in the aftermath of Hurricane Beryl, which made landfall on July 1, 2024, severely impacting the Southern Grenadines, particularly Union Island, where 90% of structures were reported damaged or destroyed. Drawing on primary data from 150 respondents collected via an online survey, the study explores the interplay between structural vulnerabilities and disaster preparedness in St. Vincent and the Grenadines. While the survey was initially intended for residents directly impacted by the hurricane, displacement and utility disruptions broadened participation to include the wider Vincentian population who experienced the event. Findings challenge dominant assumptions in disaster literature that link preparedness to sociodemographic characteristics and prior disaster experience. Although most respondents demonstrated strong awareness of hurricane risks and reported taking warnings seriously, several barriers, excluding age, gender, or relationship status, hindered effective preparedness. Insecure housing tenure, limited savings, and low insurance coverage emerged as key constraints. These results underscore the importance of viewing preparedness not solely as a matter of individual behaviour, but as a function of broader structural inequities. The study contributes to a growing body of research that reframes disaster preparedness as a development issue and calls for pro-poor, equity-centred resilience strategies, including inclusive insurance schemes, housing support, social protection, and accessible recovery mechanisms. It emphasizes the need for context-specific approaches to disaster risk reduction in SIDS and for embedding equity within climate resilience planning.

title: Exposure of Termites and Associated Microbiomes to Soil Mercury in a tropical rainforest (French Guiana)
affiliations: , , Université Paris-Saclay, INRAE, AgroParisTech, UMR SayFood,, University Paris-Est Créteil Val de Marne, , University Paris-Est Créteil Val de Marne, University Paris-Est Créteil Val de Marne, University Paris-Est Créteil Val de Marne, Sorbonne University - Institut de Recherche pour le Développement,  and University Paris-Est Créteil Val de Marne

detail.title: Exposure of Termites and Associated Microbiomes to Soil Mercury in a tropical rainforest (French Guiana)
detail.abstract: Mercury (Hg) pollution is a major concern, especially in tropical regions where artisanal and small-scale gold mining exacerbates the problem, yet its impacts on terrestrial fauna remain understudied. To assess termite exposure to Hg, we compared total Hg (THg), methylmercury (MeHg), and associated microbiomes in soil-feeders (Anoplotermes, Termes) and the wood-feeder Nasutitermes from French Guiana, along with their nests and adjacent soils. A 14-19-fold THg enrichment was observed in soil feeder bodies relative to soils and nests, compared with only 1.3-3-fold in Nasutitermes. Similarly, MeHg concentrations were higher in soil feeders, peaking in Anoplotermes and decreasing in genera with reduced soil intake. Soil-feeder gut microbiomes showed higher α-diversity than surrounding habitats. qPCR revealed higher abundances of bacteria, Hg-methylators (hgcA), and Hg-reducers (merA) in guts than in soils, with positive correlations suggesting density-dependent variation in functional groups. Gene copy numbers across compartments correlated with THg but not with body MeHg, while both Hg species influenced bacterial community structure and correlated positively with 16S rRNA OTU richness. The mechanisms underlying these relationships remain unclear. This first assessment of Hg-methylator diversity in termites reveals Desulfobacterota-related methylators as dominant in soils and nests, while Bacillota-related taxa prevail in guts with marked genus-specificity. This suggests that, with their high diversity, Isopteran guts represent a major reservoir of endemic Hg-methylators. With their prevalence and propensity to accumulate large amounts of THg and MeHg, soil-feeding termites may act as conduits of Hg to higher trophic levels and serve as effective terrestrial bioindicators of mercury exposure.

title: Taxing Mobile Money
affiliations: , International Monetary Fund (IMF) - Fiscal Affairs Department, Université d'Auvergne - Clermont 1, Centre d'Etudes et de Recherches sur le Developpement International (CERDI), Students and International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: Taxing Mobile Money

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Mobile money has become a central digital alternative to traditional banking in developing countries, yet several African governments have introduced taxes on mobile money transactions. We develop a model that characterizes how such taxes affect payment choices and generate excess burden. The model predicts that taxation reduces mobile money use, with elasticities shaped by access to substitutes and transaction costs: banked users substitute into formal alternatives, while unbanked users face higher effective costs, making the tax regressive. Taxation also induces substitution into cash, raising informality. We empirically test these predictions using cross-country survey data and novel transaction-level data from Cameroon, the Central African Republic, and Mali. Results show sharp declines in mobile money usage, with stronger responses among the banked. Unbanked and rural users bear a disproportionate burden. We use the empirical estimates to gauge the excess burden of the tax, which we quantify at 35% of revenue—highlighting its significant efficiency cost alongside its regressive impact.

title: Emerging Market Resilience
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF), International Monetary Fund (IMF), Warsaw School of Economics (SGH), International Monetary Fund, International Monetary Fund (IMF) and

detail.title: Emerging Market Resilience

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Emerging markets have shown remarkable resilience during risk-off episodes in recent years. While favorable external conditions—good luck—contributed to this resilience, improvements inpolicy frameworks—good policies—played a critical role in bolstering the capacity of emerging markets to withstand the adverse consequences of these events. Improvements in monetary policy implementation and credibility have reduced reliance on foreign exchange (FX) interventions and capital flow management measures, and stricter macroprudential regulation also contributedto less FX interventions. Also, central banks have become less sensitive to fiscal interference and hold sway over domestic borrowing conditions. Looking ahead, countries with robust frameworks face easier policy trade-offs and are better positioned to navigate risk-off episodes. In contrast, economies with weaker frameworks risk de-anchoring inflation expectations and larger output losses if monetary tightening is delayed, especially when persistent price pressures emerge. In these settings, FX interventions offer only temporary relief and are less necessary when policy frameworks are sound.

title: Trust, Confidence, and Consumption Resilience: A Quasi-natural Experiment Based on the Rural E-Commerce Demonstration County policy
affiliations: Ningbo University of Finance and Economics, Shanghai Normal University and Anhui University of Finance and Economics

detail.title: Trust, Confidence, and Consumption Resilience: A Quasi-natural Experiment Based on the Rural E-Commerce Demonstration County policy

keywords: The Rural E-Commerce Demonstration County policy

detail.abstract: This study leverages China’s Rural E-Commerce Demonstration County (REDC) policy as a quasi-natural experiment to examine how digital economics enhances rural household consumption resilience amid economic shocks. Using longitudinal data (CFPS, 2010–2018) from 11,518 households and staggered difference-in-differences models with robustness checks (parallel trends, placebo tests, and controls for concurrent policies), we quantify resilience through a multidimensional index. Results show REDC implementation increases per capita consumption resilience by 48–53%, with stronger effects in populous/commercial areas but equitable benefits across demographics. Trust-building (via secure platforms/logistics) and future confidence (from income diversification) are identified as dual mechanisms explaining 65–72% of gains. As the first causal evidence linking e-commerce to micro-level resilience, this research advances policy evaluation methodologies through entropy-weighted indices while revealing institutional-behavioral pathways. Practical implications emphasize prioritizing last-mile logistics, gender-targeted digital literacy programs, and blockchain traceability systems to sustain inclusive growth.

detail.abstract: This paper explores the evolution and determinants of sovereign debt spreads within the euro area. The analysis focuses on how a broad range of factors influenced borrowing costs for both core and peripheral member states from the run-up to the monetary union till the end of the third quarter of 2025. It traces the transition from the pre-crisis era of convergence, when sovereign risks were viewed as homogeneous, to subsequent periods of market divergence and revaluation of risk across member states. By going through periods of convergence and fragmentation, the paper demonstrates how key events governed investor perceptions and borrowing costs. The pivotal role of the European Central Bank in safeguarding monetary policy transmission and maintaining financial stability is highlighted. Notably, the research suggests that country-specific fundamentals have increasingly gained importance in investor risk assessments, challenging the usefulness of core-periphery labels. Additionally, recent sovereign spreads may more accurately reflect differentiated national risk profiles compared to the highly converged trading observed during the early years of the monetary union. While the overall range of yields has tightened, current spreads remain wider. This may indicate a more nuanced form of financial integration, one that acknowledges persistent country-specific risks and possible structural vulnerabilities within the euro area.

detail.abstract: This paper studies the role of collateral using the euro area corporate credit registry, Ana-Credit. We document key facts about the importance, distribution, and composition of collateral, including its presence, types, and values. On average, 70 % of credit amounts are collateralized. Real estate and financial assets are the most pledged, while physical movable assets and other intangible assets are less present. In addition, we show that the aggregate collateral value pledged to the banking sector is substantial, driven mainly by real estate in most countries. For the first time, we examine the collateral channel in bank credit using the actual value of individual collateral. By exploiting within- firm and within-bank variations for newly issued secured loans, we find that the elasticity of collateral value to loan commitment amounts is around 0.7-0.8. This collateral value elasticity exhibits substantial country and time heterogeneity, which can be explained by legal, financial, and macro conditions.

detail.title: Intangible Capital with Synergy and Scalability: A New Measurement Framework
detail.abstract: Scalability, the ability to expand output at low marginal cost, and synergy, the ability to combine resources to generate convex payoffs, are widely viewed as the defining features of intangible capital. Yet the current empirical measures of intangible capital implicitly rule out scalability and synergy payoffs. They rigidly mirror perpetual inventory models, created for physical capital, to linearly accumulate and amortize past research and development and selling, general, and administrative outlays. We relax these restrictions by allowing a dollar of intangible investment to generate value greater than its initial cost and by permitting investments to interact nonlinearly. We train prediction models using purchase price allocations to identifiable intangible assets in 1,533 mergers and acquisitions transactions. We apply the trained model to a broader sample of Compustat firms to estimate their intangible capital. Augmented book values of assets and equity with our estimates deliver a dramatic improvement in out-of-sample predictions of enterprise values, intrinsic returns, and patent values. We contribute to the literature by operationalizing, and proposing a method for estimating, scalability and synergy, concepts emphasized in theoretical literature, but largely ignored in firm-level estimates of internally generated intangibles.

detail.abstract:
This chapter examines China's continuous rise in the international intellectual property regime. It begins by revisiting the typology scholars have used to determine the levels at which a country engages with international norms: (1) norm breaker, (2) norm taker, (3) norm shaker and (4) norm maker. Although China has been widely considered a norm breaker or a norm taker in the intellectual property arena, the past two decades have seen China joining other like-minded countries in shaking multilateral norms. In recent years, China has also become a norm maker, ushering in new, unique policy and regulatory approaches to tackle global problems, which ranged from the COVID-19 pandemic to AI technology.
This chapter then examines four notable developments that have enabled China to shape future international intellectual property and innovation norms: (1) the negotiation of the RCEP and other nonmultilateral trade agreements, (2) the establishment of the BRI, (3) the launch of active vaccine diplomacy during the COVID-19 pandemic and (4) the assumption of global leadership in shaping AI technology and the related international regulatory environment.
The chapter further explains why China has decided to become more assertive in the intellectual property arena—a curious position for a country that has been long considered a norm breaker and a norm taker in this arena. This chapter concludes by revisiting the four questions I identified for future research in the first edition of this Handbook. The discussion explores whether these questions are still valid today—and, if so, whether the questions will yield new answers, based on China's recent developments in the intellectual property arena.

This study analyzes the validity of jobless growth in Türkiye on sectoral basis. It analyzes the impacts of agriculture, industry, construction and services sectors on unemployment using annual data for the period 2000-2022. ARDL method is applied within the scope of the analysis. The findings are tested with FMOLS and CCR methods. The results show that growth in all sectors reduces the unemployment. A one-unit increase in the share of agriculture sector in GDP decreases the unemployment rate by 0.471 points, 0.680 points in the industrial sector, 0.899 points in the construction sector and 1.383 points in the services sector in the short-run. The long-run coefficients reveal that the impacts of sectoral growth on unemployment are stronger in the long-run than in the short-run. A one unit increase in the share of the agricultural sector in GDP decreases the unemployment rate by 2.380 points, 4.057 points in the industrial sector, 1.761 points in the construction sector and 3.664 points in the services sector in the long-run. These findings show that jobless growth is not valid in Türkiye in general. On the contrary, economic growth plays an important role in reducing unemployment.

detail.abstract: Flipkart is a major Indian e-commerce platform, founded in 2007, offering products like electronics, clothing, and home goods. Flipkart has managed to connect India's wide and diverse regions with a vast network of brands and sellers through technology, logistics, and payment systems. This study explores how artificial intelligence (AI) can help improve Flipkart's reverse logistics system, which handles customer returns. The study focused on identifying common problems such as delays, communication errors, and high return costs. A simple survey was conducted among online shoppers to understand their product return experience on Flipkart. The study also used basic data such as the average return time and the reasons for the return. The results show that many problems can be reduced with the use of AI tools such as chatbots, automatic return tracking, and intelligent decision systems. The study shows that even small AI improvements can make the return process faster and easier for customers and companies. This project highlights how technology can make online shopping more efficient and user-friendly. Our findings provide guidance for Flipkart's digital strategy to help increase customer satisfaction and loyalty in India.

Regional disparities in the economic and social structures of countries have a great impact on their development levels. In geographically, culturally and economically diverse countries like Türkiye, determining the socioeconomic status of the provinces and regional differences is an important step for planning and implementing effective policies. Therefore, this study aims to determine the socioeconomic disparities of the provinces in Türkiye. For this purpose, a socioeconomic development index covering the economic and social dimensions of 81 provinces was constructed. For the index, 16 different indicators representing economic and social factors were used. These indicators were converted into indices using the Min-Max normalization method and Principal Component Analysis. Afterwards, using these indices, the provinces were divided into groups using the K-Means clustering algorithm and the Elbow method. In the last part of the study, the results are presented in a visual format using Scatter Plots, clustering maps and QGIS mapping tools. The results of the study show that 2 of the 81 provinces in Türkiye have very high, 30 high, 25 medium and 24 low socioeconomic indices. Istanbul and Ankara have very high socioeconomic status. In general, the provinces in western Türkiye have a high socioeconomic index, while the provinces in eastern and southeastern Anatolia face serious challenges in terms of socioeconomic indicators.

detail.abstract: Today, most social and economic scientists have accepted the important role of extra-economic factors such as social trust in the process of economic development of societies. According to them, public trust affects economic growth not only by creating conditions for cooperation and coordination between individuals and groups and reducing the costs of production, distribution and exchange in the economic system, but also in many other ways. This article, while examining the ways of influencing social trust on economic development, aims to provide a conceptual framework and a practical definition of social trust and its adaptation to the conditions of growth in today's Iranian society. In this research, the method of applying the model of social trust to the last four decades of Iranian society and several approaches have been used for the model of the mechanism of the effect of social trust on economic growth. The article concludes that "responsibility, efficient management, increasing business transactions, reducing possible risks in transactions, increasing domestic and foreign investment, reducing investment costs, creating welfare states" are among the influential mediating factors. are in the mechanism of social trust and economic growth.

detail.abstract: Joint investment funds, as one of the most vital non-banking financial intermediaries, are responsible for capital transfer from resource owners (society members) to consumers (manufacturing and service companies and others). In Iran, for the first time, based on the Securities Market Law, approved in 2005, joint investment funds were expected, and stock investment funds entered the capital market from the beginning of 2017. The purpose of this research was to investigate the influencing factors on the returns of stock investment funds through the analysis of the history of these funds' performances in Iran's economy. For this purpose, 136 joint funds active in the capital market were examined. Data analysis has been done with a pooled structure (unbalanced panel) and with a fixed effects regression model using the ordinary least squares (OLS) method. The results of this research confirm the existence of a significant linear relationship between fund returns and variables such as fund life, deviation from the average, ownership of all real investors, and inflation in the previous period, and market index in the previous period. Among these, the life of the fund and inflation has a negative effect on the efficiency of the fund and other variables have a positive effect.

title: Post-COP30: Technology Transfer without Access? What Belém Delivered and What it Didn't for Africa
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Post-COP30: Technology Transfer without Access? What Belém Delivered and What it Didn't for Africa
detail.abstract:
Technology transfer has long occupied a central yet unresolved place in the global climate regime. For developing countries, particularly in Africa, access to climate technologies is not a matter of innovation prestige but of survival, competitiveness, and structural transformation. From renewable energy systems and climate-resilient agriculture to early-warning infrastructure and industrial decarbonization, technology determines whether climate commitments remain aspirational or become operational.

At COP30 in Belém, Brazil, technology transfer returned to the negotiating spotlight, though largely embedded within broader discussions on finance, adaptation, and implementation. While the final negotiated text avoided explicit language on fossil fuels and delivered limited attractive breakthroughs, COP30 nonetheless introduced important institutional shifts. These included the launch of the Belém Technology Implementation Programme (TIP), the 15-year renewal of the Climate Technology Centre and Network (CTCN) through 2041, and stronger political signaling around linking technology with finance and just transition pathways.

Yet for Africa, the critical question remains unchanged: do these developments meaningfully improve access to climate technologies, or do they risk reinforcing existing asymmetries between ambition and delivery?

detail.abstract: This paper provides new evidence on how automation transforms firms' demand for skills, not by changing the occupational composition, but by reshaping what existing jobs require. Using matched data on firm-level automation investments and detailed job ads from Denmark, we extract multidimensional skill profiles through natural language processing. Guided by a task-based framework, we decompose changes in skill demand into within-and between-occupation components and find that within-occupation adjustments dominate. Automation increases the demand for soft skills in professional and managerial roles and reduces the reliance on routine hard skills in production jobs. Register data confirm parallel shifts in workforce composition: increased experience in high-skill occupations and intensified retraining among lower-skilled workers. Our findings highlight that automation reconfigures work from within, with important implications for training policy and labor market resilience.

detail.abstract: By incorporating a Cournot banking sector into a standard DSGE framework, this paper highlights a new propagation mechanism of imperfect banking competition that operates via the dynamics of the expected marginal product of capital (MPK). A higher expected return on capital implies that firms are more willing to borrow to invest in capital, making their capital and thus loan demand more inelastic. Market power enables banks to take advantage of the lower loan demand elasticity through a higher loan interest margin. Adverse shocks that tend to raise the user cost of capital and thus the expected MPK can lead to a higher loan interest margin, which in turn amplifies the output drop.

It explores the impacts on trade structures, industrial policies, and workforce dynamics. While it highlights the opportunities and challenges in their economic transformation. The key common challenges include labor market imbalances and regional disparities. Malaysia focuses on diversifying exports through trade agreements to improve its “Industry 4.0” initiative. It also addresses its challenges through education reforms and infrastructure. While Thailand relies high-tech industrialization under “Thailand 4.0”, though it faces cultural resistance and bureaucratic inefficiencies. Thailand relies on foreign talent introduction to fix demographic decline. The paper provides a framework for developing economies to handle global trade disruptions.

detail.abstract: This paper studies the role of adjustable-rate mortgages (ARMs) in monetary policy transmission within the Euro Area. Conventional wisdom holds that ARMs are relevant per se. This study finds that the presence of liquidity-constrained households strongly influences their impact. Using Euro Area survey data, I document that transmission is stronger in countries that exhibit both high ARM shares and sizable shares of liquidity-constrained households. To interpret this finding, I develop a heterogeneous-agent model featuring: (i) heterogeneity in marginal propensities to consume (MPCs), (ii) agents making both housing and mortgage choices, and (iii) a fraction of households with ARMs. In the model, MPCs determine the extent to which changes in mortgage payments translate into changes in consumption, making ARMs an important transmission vehicle only when paired with high MPCs. These results highlight that accounting for household heterogeneity in MPCs is essential to assess the strength of transmission through ARMs.

detail.title: Beyond Net Flows: Managing Gross Capital Flows under Collateral Constraints
detail.abstract: The growing importance of capital outflows from emerging economies has led to a disconnect between net and gross inflows, raising the question of whether these quantities should be analyzed separately. We study a framework in which the distinction between foreign borrowing (gross inflows) and residents’ overseas investment (gross outflows) is made explicit, in an environment with a collateral constraint where both types of flows are pledgeable. Because private agents do not internalize how their borrowing and investments jointly affect future asset prices and collateral values, their decisions generate substantial pecuniary externalities operating through both domestic and foreign asset price channels. As a result, the implied crisis probability and overborrowing extend beyond those obtained in net-flow models. We show that a set of taxes can correct the externalities, and that the interventions are considerably tighter in our environment than under net-flow regulations. Our results align with empirical evidence suggesting asymmetries in the effects of policies targeting these gross flows, as well as their interactions with global financial conditions. Overall, our setup provides a useful benchmark for assessing the potential benefits of policy prescriptions that manage separately different types of capital flows.

title: The Effect of the EU Emissions Trading System on Climate Investments

detail.title: The Effect of the EU Emissions Trading System on Climate Investments
detail.abstract: This paper analyses the effect of the European Union Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) on climate-related investments ex-post. It advances prior work by focusing on investments that directly affect regulated emissions rather than broader environmental expenditures, thereby offering a more nuanced assessment of firms' reactions to regulation. The subset of companies I focus on are German manufacturing firms that became newly regulated by the EU ETS in 2013. Using a comprehensive administrative firm-level panel dataset covering all firms with more than 20 employees, I apply a standard difference-in-differences approach to estimate the EU ETS's impact on climate investments. The results suggest that EU ETS regulation led to a statistically  significant rise in climate‑related investments, driven entirely by the extensive margin. The share of regulated firms undertaking such investments sharply increases by about 8 percentage points in the treatment period. I further explore potential drivers of this change and show that the results are robust across various specifications and sensitivity checks.

title: DuBois' Study of Black Residents of Philadelphia and a Study of Hispanics in El Paso: Discovering Heterogeneity within Urban Racialized Communities

detail.title: DuBois' Study of Black Residents of Philadelphia and a Study of Hispanics in El Paso: Discovering Heterogeneity within Urban Racialized Communities

publicationDetails.journalName: Center for Latin American & Latino Studies (CLALS) Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: The Philadelphia Negro is regarded as the first work of urban sociology to examine an urban Black community empirically. Despite being understudied by urban sociologists when Du Bois’s work was published, Black urban communities have played a significant role in U.S. culture and the field of urban sociology. Before this work, assumptions defined how people discussed black urban residents. Today, a similar pattern persists: Latino communities are integral to American society yet remain insufficiently examined in the field. Latinos are often rendered visible only through the lens of immigration status, and their contributions to urban economies are frequently viewed as secondary. Following in the DuBoisian tradition, this study analyzes data from a large NIH-funded survey of Latino residents in El Paso, Texas, a border city that is over 80% Hispanic. This analysis explores community experiences related to housing, migration history, immigrant generation, racism, and health outcomes. While the historical contexts differ, the data show how limited rights, intergenerational poverty, and labor exploitation continue to shape the lives of many Latinos, echoing themes that Du Bois identified. This paper highlights the heterogeneity of this population and underscores the need for more research on Latino urban communities in the United States.

title: Behavioral Self-Management and the Strategic Shifting of Fairness Norms
affiliations: New York University School of Law, New York University School of Law and New York University School of Law

detail.title: Behavioral Self-Management and the Strategic Shifting of Fairness Norms
detail.abstract: People often act prosocially and voluntarily conform to social and legal norms. This has fueled the idea that law can guide behavior through its expressive power. By contrast, we offer a theoretical and experimental framework suggesting that people strategically alter their decision-making environment to shift the norm applicable to their actions to one that is in their self-interest and to the detriment of others. Norm-shifting is one strategy within a broader concept we refer to as Behavioral Self-Management (BSM). To test norm-shifting, we implement a dictator game in which Allocators are offered an effort task before allocating a sum between themselves and a Recipient. Allocators receive the same endowment whether or not they work. We hypothesize that many will undertake the task to shift the applicable fairness norm from equal division to an effort-based norm that justifies their retaining a larger share. Prior evidence shows that costly effort is widely perceived as legitimizing unequal outcomes. We find that many Allocators decide to work, thereby reducing average transfers. Their work choices are strategic: their odds of working are higher the more they expect work to shift the fairness norm in their favor and the more prosocial they are-that is, the higher the moral costs they face for violating the fairness norm. Finally, Allocators who work make transfers that they expect to conform to an effort-based norm in the view of others, to maintain their self-and social-image. Our findings have implications for compliance with the law and with social norms. BSM can enable selfish non-compliance by undermining the social norms that underpin the law or by establishing social norms that provide justification for violation, while avoiding the social disapproval that would otherwise result.

title: The Aligned Economic Index & the State-Switching Model

detail.abstract: A growing empirical literature suggests that equity-premium predictability is state dependent, with much of the forecasting power concentrated around recessionary periods [10, 11, 18]. I study U.S. stock return predictability across economic regimes and document strong evidence of time-varying expected returns across both expansionary and contractionary states. I contribute in two ways. First, I introduce a stateswitching predictive regression in which the market state is defined in real time using the slope of the yield curve. Relative to the standard one-state predictive regression, the state-switching specification increases both in-sample and out-of-sample performance for the set of popular predictors considered by Welch and Goyal [32], improving the out-of-sample performance of most predictors in economically meaningful ways. Second, I propose a new aggregate predictor, the Aligned Economic Index, constructed via partial least squares (PLS). Under the state-switching model, the Aligned Economic Index exhibits statistically and economically significant predictive power in sample and out of sample, and it outperforms widely used benchmark predictors and alternative predictor-combination methods.

detail.abstract: We extend an endogenous growth model with diffusion-memory dynamics by explicitly introducing natural capital as a productive and vulnerable stock. Natural capital is degraded by economic activity and restored through regenerative investment and technological decoupling. We derive operational conditions for strong sustainability under uncertainty. We distinguish between sustainability in the arithmetic mean, which requires E[dN t /N t ] ≥ 0, and sustainability in the logarithmic mean, E[d ln N t ] ≥ 0, which explicitly incorporates environmental volatility through a penalty Itô. Environmental risk therefore raises the threshold level of technological decoupling required to preserve natural capital. We further characterize the stochastic shadow price of natural capital within a social planner problem and show how it internalizes precautionary value under uncertainty. Finally, when innovation follows a self-exciting Hawkes process, nearunstable technological regimes amplify ecological risk by increasing the probability of transitory under-decoupling episodes. The framework delivers explicit, policyrelevant sustainability thresholds for circular and regenerative growth.

title: Efficiency without Justice: The Dual Chains of Automation and Finance

detail.title: Efficiency without Justice: The Dual Chains of Automation and Finance

detail.abstract: This paper introduces the Dual Chain Theory (DCT), a moral-systems framework explaining how automation and financialization have restructured capitalism's moral foundations. The two chains-technological and financial-form interlocking feedback loops that amplify efficiency while eroding reciprocity. Their recursive interaction transforms legitimacy into a derivative of accumulation, creating what can be termed a moral entropy regime. Within this system, efficiency gains outpace moral restoration (α > 1), legitimacy becomes negatively elastic (εs < 0), and inequality (ρ > 0) replaces justice as a stabilizer. The result is a capitalism that grows by consuming its own moral resources. The paper outlines a framework for predistributive reconstruction through three corrective instruments: the Automation Dividend, the Financial Reciprocity Levy, and Universal Basic Services. Together, they aim to restore moral feedback by aligning efficiency with legitimacy. The broader claim is that capitalism's survival depends not on greater output but on the cybernetic reintegration of justice as a condition of systemic stability.

title: Financial Prediction Markets: A New Measure of Earnings Expectations
affiliations: London Business School, London Business School, Yale University and London Business School

detail.title: Financial Prediction Markets: A New Measure of Earnings Expectations
detail.abstract: We construct a high-frequency measure of earnings expectations using financial prediction markets. Unlike analyst forecasts, which are updated infrequently and prone to agency conflicts, prediction market prices reflect real-time, stake-backed beliefs. Each contract pays one dollar if realized earnings exceed the analyst consensus; we derive the conditions under which these prices represent subjective probabilities and introduce a methodology to convert them into implied expectations about earnings. Relative to analyst forecasts, we find that market-implied expectations are (i) more accurate; (ii) incrementally informative for earnings announcement returns; and (iii) significantly less biased, though they exhibit short-term overreaction in contrast to the underreaction typical of analysts. Our current sample covers the market's inception from September 15, 2025, through November 15, 2025; we will regularly update this analysis as new contracts resolve. We expect this measure to become increasingly informative as the market matures, liquidity deepens, and financial prediction markets become part of mainstream finance.

title: Ground-mounted solar and the impact of land-use planning: evidence from France

detail.title: Ground-mounted solar and the impact of land-use planning: evidence from France
detail.abstract: Access to suitable land is critical for the deployment of renewable energy. This paper provides new causal evidence on how land-use regulation affects the development of ground-mounted solar photovoltaic (PV) installations. I combine a dataset on changes in zoning regulation at the municipality level in France with information on the commissioning of solar PV installations. Using a staggered difference-in-differences design, I show that adopting more detailed zoning regulations facilitates the development of solar PV, due to better alignment with national policies. Conversely, when zoning decisions are made at the inter-municipality level, i.e. among grouped municipalities, regulations become more restrictive toward solar PV development. Mechanisms suggest that this is due to changes in governance and in the distribution of tax revenues among constituent municipalities upon the transfer of authority to the inter-municipality. The results suggest that the decentralization of land-use planning may hamper the efficiency of the spatial deployment of renewable energy.

title: The QFlex Distribution

detail.title: The QFlex Distribution

declarations.funderStatement: Center for Engineering and Decision Analytics

detail.abstract: Quantile-parameterized distributions (QPDs) are widely used in decision analysis because expert judgments are naturally expressed in terms of quantiles. Existing QPD families such as the Metalog offer considerable flexibility but lack analytic monotonicity guarantees, requiring ex post numerical repair. This paper introduces the QFlex distribution, a new QPD system constructed entirely from monotone transformations of valid quantile functions. QFlex interleaves powers of exponential, reflected-exponential, and centered-uniform quantile bases, yielding a flexible expansion that remains monotone under simple coefficient conditions. We show that QFlex has a full-rank design matrix under mild assumptions, can interpolate any finite set of quantile assessments, and converges to the target quantile function as the number of terms increases. When all coefficients are nonnegative, QFlex is strictly increasing and unimodal; additional modes arise only in a structured and controllable manner. A comprehensive comparison across approximately 3,500 Pearson-system distributions demonstrates that QFlex generally matches or exceeds the accuracy of the Metalog distribution at moderate orders while offering explicit analytic monotonicity conditions. A synthetic example illustrates QFlex's practical advantage: valid fits can be enforced directly through simple coefficient constraints, avoiding the complex post-fit monotonicity repair required by the Metalog distribution.

publicationDetails.detailsText: European Corporate Governance Institute – Finance Working Paper No. 1116/2025

detail.abstract: We study the Panic of 1907 to understand how opaque corporate governance and loose market regulation can render financial systems susceptible to financial crises. Using a new daily dataset for all stocks traded on the New York Stock Exchange between 1905 and 1910, we study the impact of information asymmetry during the Panic of 1907- one of the most severe financial crises of the 20th century. We estimate that the acute liquidity freeze drove up the median spread from 0.8% to 3% during the peak of the crisis in October of that year. Spreads rose most among mining companies-the industry with the worst track record of corporate governance and the epicenter of the rumors that triggered runs on several financial institutions with links to a notorious firm in the sector. Stocks of the highly-regulated railroad firms and companies with close ties to Wall Street’s “Money Trust” weathered the crisis with the greatest trading liquidity. We find other hallmarks of information-based illiquidity: trading volume dropped and price impact rose. Despite short-term cash infusions into the market, the market remained relatively illiquid for several months following the peak of the panic. Thus, our findings demonstrate how opaque systems allow idiosyncratic rumors to spread and amplify into a long-lasting, market-wide crisis. Asset pricing tests suggest that sophisticated traders recognized and incorporated liquidity considerations in their pricing of market risk.

detail.abstract: Digital payment systems are increasingly recognized not just as transaction conduits but as foundational information infrastructures that shape how small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) access finance, especially across borders. Yet much of the existing literature treats payment technologies and SME financing as separate domains, missing the critical linkages between infrastructure design, data flows, and credit outcomes. This article addresses that gap by proposing and elaborating a novel four-layer conceptual framework that connects (1) payment infrastructures, (2) data and access regimes, (3) financing intermediation models, and (4) SMElevel outcomes-with explicit attention to cross-border contexts and the divergent trajectories of emerging and developed economies. Drawing on Nigeria and Poland as illustrative cases, the framework demonstrates how mobile-first, platform-centric ecosystems in emerging markets differ structurally and functionally from the bank-integrated, regulation-driven systems of developed economies like those in the EU. The analysis shows that while both models can support domestic SME financing through real-time data and embedded credit, their capacity to enable cross-border finance hinges on interoperability, data portability, and regulatory alignment-areas where global fragmentation persists. The article contributes to theory by reframing digital payments as sociotechnical information systems rather than neutral rails, and to practice by offering a diagnostic tool for policymakers, central banks, and FinTech providers seeking to design more inclusive, interoperable SME finance ecosystems. It concludes with concrete recommendations for research, regulation, and infrastructure investment that prioritize SME usability, data liquidity, and crossborder coherence.

detail.abstract: Institutions designed to manage risk often rely on formal signals documentation, escalation protocols, and legal thresholds to determine when action is warranted. However, human suffering does not always present in ways that align with institutional recognition systems. This paper examines how pain that is visible, acute, and real can nevertheless remain operationally invisible when it falls outside documented pathways of credibility. Using healthcare as a representative environment, the analysis explores how institutions respond to suffering that lacks procedural validation, and how this gap contributes to moral injury, public mistrust, and systemic harm. The paper argues that unrecognized pain is not an anomaly but a predictable outcome of systems that prioritize defensibility over responsiveness.

detail.abstract: The SNB implements its monetary policy by using several instruments, including repurchase agreement (repo) transactions. title: Financial Inclusion, Fintech, and Inequality

detail.title: Financial Inclusion, Fintech, and Inequality
detail.abstract: This study investigates the distributional consequences of financial inclusion and fintech adoption in advanced economies, focusing on the G10 countries over 1990-2023. Combining a multi-layered conceptual framework with dynamic panel estimations, the analysis explores whether financial technology amplifies or mitigates inequality under different institutional conditions. The results provide three central insights. First, financial inclusion exerts a consistently inequality-reducing effect across income and wealth indicators, supporting theories that link access to finance with expanded opportunity sets, enhanced consumption smoothing, and greater resilience to economic shocks. Second, fintech adoption demonstrates nonlinear and threshold-dependent behaviour: in low-inclusion environments, fintech reinforces structural inequalities by favouring digitally integrated and higher-income households, whereas in highly inclusive systems, fintech reduces inequality by lowering transaction costs, broadening access to credit, and intensifying competition in financial markets. Third, the interaction between inclusion and fintech is the dominant channel through which distributional outcomes are shaped, indicating strong institutional complementarities. Wealth inequality dynamics further reveal that fintech disproportionately benefits capital-rich households unless paired with asset-access mechanisms. The findings contribute to macro-finance, development economics, and institutional political economy by demonstrating that the distributional effects of digital finance are endogenous to the institutional architecture of modern financial systems. Policy implications emphasise the importance of inclusive digital infrastructures, algorithmic fairness, and assetbuilding mechanisms to ensure that technological innovation promotes rather than undermines equitable economic development.

The inconsistent precedent left courts to experiment, until an attempt at coherence was imposed by the decision in Prest v Petrodel. However, this decision embodied bold and arguably hasty logic which sparked a contentious debate with respect to its assistance to the doctrine. Accordingly, this article will analyse Prest v Petrodel, the shortcomings of the decision, the impact on the uncertainties of the doctrine, and provide noteworthy commentary with regard to the Caribbean's indigenous jurisprudence.

title: Earnings Calls and Echo Chambers: Evidence from the Introduction of Livestreaming on StockTwits

detail.abstract: We examine whether improved access to firm disclosures weakens social media echo chambers, using the introduction of livestreamed earnings calls on StockTwits as a shock. We find that call streaming is associated with lower selective following, reduced exposure to confirmatory content, and belief revision over the following 30 days. Both call content and real-time chats contribute, with the strongest effects when calls surface disconfirming information and chats are active and diverse. The findings suggest that reducing frictions to accessing primary information and increasing exposure to diverse views can help mitigate the consequences of echo chambers in financial markets.

detail.abstract: This research aims to explore the governance of European Union (EU) infrastructures through the lens of a unified framework, emphasizing the role of the Task Force Infrastructure4Europe as a catalyst for continental unification. The study addresses key research questions, including how to effectively integrate infrastructure governance to enhance cohesion among member states, the impact of the Task Force on infrastructure initiatives, and the prioritization of sustainability and resilience in infrastructure development. Findings indicate that a unified governance structure can significantly improve coordination and resource allocation, thereby addressing regional disparities and enhancing strategic autonomy. The research highlights the importance of stakeholder engagement, revealing that inclusive mechanisms can foster collaboration and ensure that diverse perspectives are considered in infrastructure planning. Additionally, the economic implications of a cohesive governance framework suggest that long-term investments in infrastructure yield substantial benefits, while policy recommendations emphasize the need for adaptive decision-making to respond to emerging challenges. Overall, the study concludes that integrating EU infrastructure governance into a single framework is essential for achieving continental unification, enhancing resilience, and positioning the EU as a strategic actor on the global stage. By prioritizing sustainability and stakeholder engagement, the EU can create a robust infrastructure system that supports long-term economic and social objectives. A central feature of this initiative is the promotion of continental unification, both politically and financially. By aligning infrastructure strategies across all Member States, the EU can strengthen its cohesion, reduce disparities, and ensure equitable access to strategic digital, energy, and transport networks. Financially, unified planning and investment reduce duplication, maximize efficiency, and create economies of scale for Europe's largest infrastructure projects. By establishing the TF-I4Europe, the Commission can ensure that Europe's infrastructure policies are strategically coherent, efficiently implemented, financially optimized, and politically cohesive.

detail.abstract: Modern technology is diffusing at unprecedented scale and speed across the globe, driving significant economic transformations in the 21st century. This paper examines how rapid technological diffusion-particularly digital technologies such as mobile internet, broadband connectivity, satellite communications, and artificial intelligence (AI)-is accelerating economic growth in developing nations and reshaping living standards worldwide. We present a datadriven analysis of impacts on productivity, labor markets, entrepreneurship, infrastructure, and global trade, with a focus on the Global South. The historical context of technology adoption is contrasted with the current era's accelerated diffusion, enabled by ubiquitous mobile devices and internet access. We then analyze regional economic outcomes: Asia's digital boom, Africa's leapfrogging via mobile systems, Latin America's growing online economy, the Middle East/North Africa's mixed progress, and other developing regions. Despite clear gains-higher productivity, new jobs, improved household welfare, and expanded trade-challenges persist in the form of digital divides, skill gaps, and inequalities. We discuss how unequal access and readiness can widen income disparities and exclude vulnerable groups. Looking ahead, the paper explores future prospects and policy implications to ensure that modernization at scale remains inclusive and sustainable. Policy measures are outlined for investing in infrastructure, expanding digital access, upskilling labor, fostering entrepreneurship, and strengthening governance of emerging technologies. In conclusion, while rapid technology diffusion is a powerful engine of growth and improved living standards, deliberate policies are required to bridge remaining divides and maximize benefits for all.

detail.abstract: Modern civilisation is undergoing a profound transformation driven by the pursuit of systemic efficiency. Advances in automation, artificial intelligence (AI), data analytics, and cybernetic feedback systems are enabling unprecedented optimization across governance, economics, and technology. This paper argues that the 21st century marks an "Age of Optimization" in which societies approach near-optimal performance through innovation and intelligent feedback infrastructures. We trace the historical evolution of optimization from the industrial era's focus on mechanization and efficiency to today's information-driven paradigms. We examine how automation and AI reduce inefficiencies and enable anticipatory governance, how feedback loops and cybernetic principles inform modern institutions, and the implications of near-optimal systems for society, the economy, and human autonomy. While optimization promises great gains, we also highlight the risks of over-optimization-including systemic fragility, the erosion of human values, and ethical convergence toward narrow objectives. Finally, we discuss philosophical and strategic questions posed by approaching the "efficiency frontier" of society: What should remain unoptimized to preserve resilience, creativity, and human dignity? The paper synthesizes insights from systems theory, information science, economics and governance, supported by contemporary research and real-world examples. Throughout, we maintain a scholarly, rigorous analysis with the aim of informing both academic discourse and practical decision-making in this new era of optimization.

title: Solving the Forecast Combination Puzzle
affiliations: University of California, Riverside (UCR) and University of California, Riverside (UCR)

detail.title: Solving the Forecast Combination Puzzle
detail.abstract: This paper addresses the forecast combination puzzle-the empirical observation that a simple average of individual forecasts, using equal weights, often outperforms more sophisticated combination methods. We propose a novel forecast combination approach designed to improve upon the simple average, particularly when the number of forecasts is large relative to the sample size. In our framework, the simple average is treated as a common factor shared across all individual forecasts. We then identify additional common factors and idiosyncratic components that enhance the predictive content beyond that captured by the simple average. Empirical applications in macroeconomic forecasting demonstrate that our method yields more accurate forecasts than the simple average and helps resolve the forecast combination puzzle. The procedure can be started with any combined forecast and iterated until no further improvement is achieved.

title: Anti-tax Avoidance Rules and the Real Effects on Foreign Investors

detail.title: Anti-tax Avoidance Rules and the Real Effects on Foreign Investors
detail.abstract: As the economy continues to shift toward globalization, investment from foreign sources is becoming increasingly important for economic stimulation, human capital, employment, and technology advancements. Tax policy is one tool policymakers use to attract foreign investment. However, tax policy is also often used to limit tax avoidance, which can increase the after-tax cost of investing in a country. This study investigates the real effects of prominent anti-tax avoidance measures likely to affect foreign investors-specifically, the OECD's Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS) initiative, interest deduction limitations, transfer pricing regulations, and general anti-avoidance rules-on inward foreign direct investment (FDI) in countries that have adopted these policies. We document that these anti-tax avoidance policies have a negative effect on foreign investment, with nuanced effects on both debt-versus equitybased investments. Additional analyses show that the decline in FDI growth relates to real investment, highlighting a perhaps unintended consequence of anti-avoidance rules. Cross-sectional analyses further show that the FDI reductions following the enactment of anti-avoidance rules correspond to FDI increases in lower-income countries.

detail.abstract: Removing barriers to competition across the economy would drive strong, sustainable and inclusive growth while maintaining fiscal discipline. This paper recommends that federal, provincial and territorial governments come together to agree on a 10-year pro-competitive reform agenda. The agenda would be based on three pillars: 1) a systematic review of regulations through a competition lens based on agreed timelines and review parameters; 2) an opt-in federal transfer scheme to incentivize delivery of provincial/territorial reforms; and 3) a dedicated accountability unit to monitor and report on outcomes. The initiative would leverage existing institutions, and transfers would be tied to anticipated federal revenue gains from qualifying reforms, ensuring fiscal responsibility. This proposal targets the biggest drag on productivity in Canada, oKers a practical path to overcoming inertia, and draws on models that have succeeded abroad. It would work here, too.

title: The Effect and Impact mechanism of Low Carbon Pilot Cities on Corporate Productivity: Evidence from China
